written.myAnswer: Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions occurring in an organism. Catabolism breaks complex molecules into simpler ones and releases energy; anabolism builds complex molecules from simpler ones and requires energy.
Anabolism requires an input of energy, for example, the synthesis of proteins from amino acids.
An enzyme is a biological catalyst, usually a protein, that speeds up metabolic reactions without being consumed.
The active site is the region of an enzyme where the substrate binds and the reaction occurs. Its shape allows it to bind specific substrate(s), giving the enzyme its specificity.
Increasing substrate concentration increases enzyme activity until the enzyme’s active sites are saturated; then the reaction rate reaches a maximum.
Pepsin works optimally at a low, acidic pH, while trypsin works optimally at a high, alkaline pH.
An enzyme’s optimum temperature and optimum pH are the temperature and pH at which it works at its maximum rate.
Competitive inhibitors bind to and block the active site, competing with the substrate. Non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and alter the enzyme’s shape or activity.
Enzymes are biological catalysts, primarily proteins. They speed up metabolic reactions without being consumed, are specific to their substrates, and work best at optimum temperature and pH.

Low temperatures slow enzyme and substrate movement, reducing successful collisions and activity. Above the optimum temperature, heat alters the enzyme’s shape, including its active site, so the substrate no longer fits properly. The enzyme becomes denatured and its activity is greatly reduced or stops.
Each enzyme has an optimum pH at which it works fastest. A pH above or below that optimum can alter the active site and reduce substrate binding and activity; extreme pH may denature the enzyme.

Enzyme activity is affected by temperature, pH, substrate concentration and inhibitors. Activity rises with temperature up to an optimum, while excess heat can denature the enzyme. Each enzyme has an optimum pH; deviations can alter the active site. More substrate increases the rate until active sites are saturated. Competitive inhibitors block the active site, while non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and alter enzyme activity.

In the Lock-and-Key model, the enzyme’s active site has a fixed shape complementary to the substrate. In the Induced Fit model, the active site is flexible and changes shape as the substrate binds. Both models explain enzyme-substrate specificity and formation of the enzyme-substrate complex.
